title: Jeremiah 20:14–18
context: Immediately after his praise, Jeremiah curses the day of his birth and the man who brought the news of it, and asks why he came out of the womb only to see trouble and shame. The lament closely resembles Job 3. Both traditions read it as the anguished cry of a faithful servant under great pressure, preserved in Scripture to give voice to deep sorrow, not as a doctrinal statement or a model to follow, and not as a settled despair over God’s faithfulness.

verses.text: Cursed is the day in which I was born. Don’t let the day in which my mother bore me be blessed.
verses.arminianNotes: Cursed is the day in which I was born. Arminian readers see a man in deep anguish voicing his pain honestly before God, not renouncing his faith but crying out from its depths.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the close parallel with Job 3:1-3, where Job also curses the day of his birth. Both traditions read the words as lament, not as a curse on God. The verse curses the day of his birth; the notes do not settle what else he did or did not wish.

verses.text: Cursed is the man who brought news to my father, saying, “A boy is born to you,” making him very glad.
verses.arminianNotes: Cursed is the man who brought news to my father, Arminian readers see the curse directed at the day and the messenger, not at his parents or at God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the bitterness is poetic and focused on the circumstances of his birth. The language expresses grief rather than a literal wish for harm to an unnamed messenger.

verses.text: Let that man be as the cities which the LORD overthrew, and didn’t repent. Let him hear a cry in the morning, and shouting at noontime,
verses.arminianNotes: Let that man be as the cities which the LORD overthrew, and didn’t repent. Arminian readers note that the cities are commonly understood as Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:25), though they are not named here.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the language is poetic hyperbole, the extremity of grief rather than a reasoned petition. Scripture preserves such words without commending them as models.

verses.text: because he didn’t kill me from the womb. So my mother would have been my grave, and her womb always great.
verses.arminianNotes: Because he didn’t kill me from the womb. Arminian readers hear Jeremiah cursing the day of his birth, a cry that recalls Job 3:11, spoken by one weighed down by his calling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that the LORD had called Jeremiah before birth (1:5). These words sit in tension with God’s purpose for him in 1:5, and the book lets that tension stand.

verses.text: Why did I come out of the womb to see labor and sorrow, that my days should be consumed with shame?
verses.arminianNotes: Why did I come out of the womb to see labor and sorrow, Arminian readers see the chapter ending with an unanswered question, the honest voice of suffering that God allows to be heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the lament ends without resolution, yet Jeremiah continues his ministry in the chapters that follow. Both traditions read the cry pastorally as permission to bring the darkest sorrow to God.
